findings.reality: The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline — the spec's own primary clinical anchor — recommends the 75g OGTT as the most accurate test to assess glycaemic status in PCOS/PMOS regardless of BMI, with fasting glucose and/or HbA1c as reduced-accuracy fallbacks. CGM appears nowhere as a recommended assessment. The spec's supporting citation is a conference abstract (ENDO 2025, jendso supplement) plus a pilot study — feasibility-grade evidence, not a recommendation. So the single most expensive and most hardware-dependent feature in the document is also the least guideline-anchored. An OGTT at Thyrocare costs ₹100–₹300; a month of CGM costs ~₹8,400. The cheap option is the one the guideline actually endorses.
findings.evidence: 2023 Guideline recommendation: "the 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) [is] the most accurate test to assess glycaemic status in PCOS, regardless of BMI"; fasting glucose/HbA1c only "if an OGTT cannot be performed... noting significantly reduced accuracy." Thyrocare GTT (2 hour) listed at ₹100; 75g GTT ₹300.
findings.correction: Replace the CGM feature with a guideline-aligned, zero-hardware substitute: an "OGTT readiness + result-logging" flow (already half-present as §3.6 'OGTT reminder + prep guide'). Reframe the pitch line from "we make insulin resistance visible daily" to "we make sure the one test that actually measures it gets done, prepped for, and tracked over years" — which is both cheaper and more defensible.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.3 "Wearable import — Apple Health / Google Fit / Samsung Health sync: sleep stages, steps, resting HR, HRV, SpO₂" (v1, P1)
findings.reality: Of those five data types, only steps are producible by a phone alone. iPhone alone records time in bed, not sleep stages; sleep stages (Awake/REM/Core/Deep), resting heart rate and HRV all require an Apple Watch. The same holds on Android: Health Connect is a data layer, not a sensor — it contains sleep stages, RHR, HRV and SpO₂ only if some wearable wrote them. The spec tags this v1/P1 and then makes downstream v1 features depend on it: 'Phase-normalized HR/HRV baselines' (v1), 'Sleep regularity tracking' (v1), 'Overnight HR trend (wearable)' (v2), and §5.4 lists 'Sleep stages — Wearable import — v1' as a named signal. This is a silent hardware assumption sitting inside the v1 milestone, not a v2 nice-to-have.
findings.evidence: Apple Support: "iPhone... can only track time in bed while the Apple Watch tracks time asleep (Awake, REM, Core, Deep sleep)"; resting heart rate is computed by Apple Watch from all-day heart rate sampling.
findings.correction: Retag wearable import as "Optional enrichment — Later/P3, zero features depend on it." Rewrite the v1 line to: "Steps/movement from phone pedometer (CMPedometer / Health Connect StepsRecord) — phone-only." Substitute the phone-only path for the rest: resting HR from the active finger-PPG check (§3.3, already v1/P1), sleep timing from user-declared bed/wake plus the circadian unlock-timestamp proxy, and delete sleep *stages* entirely — no phone-only substitute exists and none is needed for the coaching lever, which is regularity, not architecture.

findings.claimOrFeature: "Google Fit" named as a sync target in §3.3, §6.2 (node E1) and §6.8 (consent C6)
findings.reality: Google Fit APIs are being retired. Google blocked all new developer sign-ups on 1 May 2024 — a team starting this product in 2026 literally cannot obtain Google Fit API access. Existing access is supported only until the end of 2026, and Google states there is no direct replacement for the Fit REST API. The correct targets are Health Connect (Android-only, on-device) and Apple HealthKit (iOS); for cloud/web there is no equivalent. Shipping a spec in July 2026 that names Google Fit as a v1 integration is naming a platform that will be dead before v1 ships.
findings.evidence: Android Developers, Google Fit migration FAQ: "Developers cannot sign up to use these APIs as of May 1, 2024"; "Google Fit APIs will be supported until the end of 2026"; "there's no direct replacement for the Fit REST API."
findings.correction: Global find-and-replace: "Apple Health / Google Fit / Samsung Health" → "Apple HealthKit (iOS) / Health Connect (Android)". Add the platform asymmetry note the spec currently hides: Health Connect is Android-only and has no web/PWA equivalent, so the PWA distribution channel gets zero wearable data by construction.

findings.claimOrFeature: Implicit assumption that reading sleep/HRV/SpO₂ from the platform health store is a routine integration for a 4-person team
findings.reality: Health Connect read access is not self-serve. Every data type must be declared and justified in a Play Console 'Health apps' form on the App content page, and access to sensitive types requires approval — apps that skip this are blocked at runtime. Google's guidance requires requesting only what supports a specific user-facing feature and documenting the reason per data type. Policy tightened further: the August 2025 Health policy update made the Health Apps Declaration mandatory, and January 2026 enforcement added a 'Medical Device' labeling system and stricter Health Connect data justifications. An app that reads HRV/SpO₂ and then shows an OSA screen and a 'Metabolic Weather' state is exactly the profile that draws reviewer scrutiny on the medical-device question.
findings.evidence: Android Developers, Declare access to Health Connect data types: "you must declare your app's data use as well as declare access to the Health Connect data types that your app uses. Users might be prompted with an error message where your app can't access the Health Connect data types because they require special approval." Play Console Health apps policy, Jan 2026 enforcement adds medical-device labeling.
findings.correction: Add a row to §9 Regulatory & Safety Guardrails: "Play Console Health Apps Declaration + per-data-type Health Connect justification is a gating dependency on any release that reads platform health data; budget 2–4 weeks of review latency and a possible rejection." And prefer requesting the narrowest set (steps only) precisely to avoid the medical-device labeling trap.

findings.claimOrFeature: Wearable import as a realistic data source for the stated primary user: Indian women 16–35
findings.reality: India's wearable market is contracting, and the part of it that grew is the part that produces the least trustworthy data. IDC: India wearables fell 4.0% YoY in 2025 to 114.2M units, with smartwatch shipments down 17.6% to 28.9M; Noise (26.6%), boAt (14.1%) and Fire-Boltt (9.7%) hold ~50%+ of smartwatch share, and the sub-₹5,000 price band grew its share 87%. These budget companion apps (NoiseFit, Fire-Boltt Fit) have no documented Health Connect integration — one Fire-Boltt app was pulled from Play in 2024 — so their data is often unreachable even if the user owns the watch. And where the data is reachable, sleep staging is the weakest output even on premium devices: PSG-validated studies find acceptable accuracy for total sleep time and sleep efficiency but limited capability for stage detection, with further degradation in insomnia and OSA populations — the exact population this product targets (37% OSA prevalence claimed in §2.2).
findings.evidence: IDC via BizTechReports: India wearables -4.0% to 114.2M units in 2025; smartwatch shipments -17.6% to 28.9M; Noise 26.6%, boAt 14.1%, Fire-Boltt 9.7%; sub-₹5,000 share +87%. SLEEP Advances PSG validation of six consumer wearables: sleep-stage detection capability "remains limited"; lower accuracy in insomnia and lower sensitivity in OSA patients.
findings.correction: Kill the competitive-matrix implication that wearable integration is a strength. Replace it with the honest positioning that is actually differentiating: "Works on a ₹10,000 phone with no watch, no sensor, no strips. Every competitor's metabolic layer needs hardware our user does not own." That is a better India-first pitch than a wearable checkbox.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.6 "Home glucose log (optional) — CGM or glucometer readings correlated with meals/mood" (v2, P2)
findings.reality: A glucometer is cheap to acquire but not cheap to use: meters run ~₹500–1,500 and strips ₹8–15 each (Accu-Chek Active 50 strips ₹899; OneTouch Select 25 strips ₹395), with proprietary strip lock-in per brand. Meaningful post-meal glucose profiling needs several pricks per day — a recurring consumable cost plus a painful, adherence-hostile ritual for a non-diabetic wellness user. Marking it "(optional)" does not exempt it: §6.7's Metabolic Weather fusion and §3.14's 'Glucose-response meal tagging' both consume glucose as an input, so the optional feature is quietly load-bearing for two non-optional ones.
findings.evidence: Accu-Chek Active 50 strips ₹899 (Moglix); OneTouch Select 25 strips from ₹395; per-strip range ₹8–15 with proprietary strip/meter lock-in.
findings.correction: There is no phone-only substitute for a glucose value — say so plainly rather than substituting a fake one. Replace 'Glucose-response meal tagging' with 'Meal-archetype → symptom tagging': the AI meal snap classifies high-GL vs low-GL Indian meal archetypes (phone-only), and the n-of-1 engine correlates that against her self-reported 2–4h energy crash, craving and skin outcomes. Copy must change from "your glucose rose 40 mg/dL after this meal" (impossible without hardware, and a quasi-clinical claim) to "meals like this are followed by an energy dip for you, 7 of 9 times."

findings.claimOrFeature: Blood pressure — §3.6 screening ledger "BP annually" and §3.14 "Pulse transit time (PTT) BP trend" (Later, P3)
findings.reality: Two different things, and only one is a violation. (a) "BP annually" in the screening ledger is a reminder to have BP measured by a clinician/pharmacy — a referral, not a hardware dependency; acceptable, same category as labs. (b) PTT-based BP from dual PPG is research-stage and, framed as any kind of BP output, drifts straight into regulated territory. (c) Critically, the only consumer product that comes close — Samsung Health Monitor — is not a counter-example but proof of the barrier: it requires a Galaxy Watch AND recalibration against an upper-arm cuff-based monitor every 28 days, is first-party Samsung only (no third-party API), CDSCO-cleared as a regulated feature in India, and its availability varies by country. That is a two-device dependency plus a regulatory clearance a 4-person team will not obtain.
findings.evidence: Samsung support: "After you have calibrated your Galaxy Watch with an upper-arm, cuff-based blood pressure monitor... You won't need to use the cuff-based monitor again until the next calibration in 28 days." India rollout was via CDSCO clearance on Galaxy Watch 4/5/6 series.
findings.correction: Keep "BP annually" in the screening ledger, explicitly labelled "measured at a clinic or pharmacy — we do not measure BP." Delete the PTT BP trend row entirely rather than leaving it at Later/P3: an unclaimed research row in a spec becomes a promised feature in a deck, and BP is the single fastest way to lose the non-SaMD framing in §9.

findings.claimOrFeature: Lab tests (fasting insulin, OGTT, lipids, vitamin D, HbA1c) — §3.6 Lab vault, Guideline screening ledger, Test-request helper, Vitamin D test-then-correct
findings.reality: Ruling: labs are NOT a violation of the no-external-devices rule, and this is not a close call. The rule exists to stop the product from being unusable unless the user buys and operates hardware the product tells her to buy. Labs fail every prong of that test: (1) she buys a one-off service, not a device she owns and operates; (2) the tests are mandated for every PMOS patient by the 2023 International Guideline whether or not this app exists — the app is a reminder layer over pre-existing routine care, not a demand generator; (3) costs are one-off and low in India (fasting insulin ~₹800 at Dr Lal PathLabs; 75g GTT ₹300 and 2-hour GTT ₹100 at Thyrocare; 25-OH vitamin D ₹700–1,300, with free home phlebotomy collection widely offered); (4) decisively, the lab *features* deliver their full value to a user who never gets a single test — 'Test-request helper', 'Question scripts' and 'Building My Case' produce an advocacy artifact from zero lab data. Compare CGM, which produces literally nothing without a ₹4,349 purchase. Two caveats that must be written into the spec, or the ruling flips.
findings.evidence: 2023 Guideline mandates OGTT/glycaemic screening, lipids and BP for PMOS independent of any app. India pricing: fasting insulin ~₹800 (Dr Lal PathLabs listing); Thyrocare 2-hour GTT ₹100, 75g GTT ₹300, 25-OH Vitamin D (Total) ₹700–1,300 with free home collection.
findings.correction: Add an explicit ruling paragraph to §3.6: "Lab tests are referrals into routine guideline-mandated care, not a product hardware dependency. Two hard constraints follow: (a) no n-of-1 pattern, experiment verdict, coaching lever, insight, or doctor export may be gated behind any lab value — the Lab vault is optional enrichment and every downstream feature must degrade gracefully to zero labs; (b) 'Vitamin D test-then-correct' must never block the supplement education flow on a test result." Also promote 'Test-request helper' (currently MVP/P0) in the pitch — it is the highest-leverage feature in the entire document precisely because it costs the user nothing and needs no hardware.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.14 "Metabolic Weather daily card — Fuses RHR + HRV + sleep + steps + glucose" and §6.7 fusion flow (7 declared input signals); plus "Confidence-gated insight fusion — surface pattern only when ≥2 signal types agree"
findings.reality: Under the no-external-device rule the fusion card loses 2 of its 7 declared inputs outright (Glucose CV — needs CGM; Sleep stages — needs a wearable) and degrades 2 more (RHR and HRV drop from continuous wearable sampling to sparse, opt-in, consent-gated phone PPG samples). What actually survives phone-only: phone step count, user-declared bed/wake regularity, self-reported energy/mood, probabilistic cycle phase, and intermittent camera/finger PPG. That is still enough for a daily state card — but the card must be rebuilt around those five, not around the seven currently drawn in §6.7. The knock-on matters more: 'Confidence-gated insight fusion' requires ≥2 independent signal types to agree, and once glucose and wearable sleep are removed, the count of genuinely independent phone-derivable signal types is thin enough that the gate will suppress most insights — which is correct behaviour but destroys the promised insight volume against the §10 target of >1.5 pattern reveals/user/week.
findings.evidence: Spec §6.7 declares inputs RHR, HRV, SLEEP, STEPS, GLUC, MOOD, PHASE; §5.4 sources 'Glucose variability — CGM import (Stelo/Libre)' and 'Sleep stages — Wearable import'; both are external-hardware-only per the findings above.
findings.correction: Redraw the §6.7 diagram with exactly the phone-derivable inputs: phone steps, declared sleep timing + circadian regularity, self-reported energy/mood, cycle phase, and opt-in PPG-derived RHR/HRV with confidence weights. Add a line: "Glucose and wearable sleep stages are not inputs; the card is defined without them." Then re-derive the §10 pattern-reveal targets from the reduced signal set instead of inheriting numbers computed against a seven-signal fusion.

findings.claimOrFeature: How much of the "innovative" v2 pillar (§3.14, 23 features) collapses when external devices are removed?
findings.reality: Less than the framing suggests — and this is the audit's most useful positive finding. Of the 23 rows in §3.14, exactly 2 are hard external-device dependencies (CGM/OTC glucose sync; Glucose-response meal tagging) = ~9%. Two more are degraded-not-killed (Metabolic Weather fusion; Confidence-gated insight fusion). The other 19 — PHRM passive HR, opportunistic re-sampling, finger PPG SpO₂, contactless respiratory rate, bedside BCG, snoring audio, camera stress, AI meal snap, skin biomarker AI, hirsutism density, voice biomarker, circadian score, smart nudge timing, HRV biofeedback, Gemini RAG, brain-fog proxy, PTT BP, federated learning, digital control arm — are all phone-only by construction. In the §4 Phase 2 ship list, 1 of 12 items dies (CGM sync). By contrast §3.3 Passive & Physiological Monitoring loses or degrades 3 of 8 rows (wearable import; overnight HR wearable; the wearable-fed portion of sleep regularity), and §5.4's signal table loses 2 of 12. So the device rule costs v1 more than v2. Caveat, stated plainly: this finding says only that the surviving v2 features need no hardware. Whether they are *reliable* is a separate audit — several (BCG, contactless rRR, camera stress, PTT BP, brain-fog proxy) are research-grade, and 'phone-only' is not the same as 'shippable'.
findings.evidence: Feature-by-feature classification of §3.14's 23 rows and §4 Phase 2's 12-item ship list against the hardware criterion, cross-checked with the CGM and wearable findings above.
findings.correction: Add a short subsection '§3.14.1 Hardware posture' stating: "21 of 23 innovative features require nothing but the phone. We removed the 2 that did not (CGM sync, glucose-response meal tagging). No feature in this product requires a purchase." Then move the device-dependent rows into §8 Anti-Features as item 14: 'No feature that requires buying hardware — no wearable, no CGM, no glucometer, no cuff.' Turning the constraint into a stated anti-feature is both honest and a stronger differentiator than the wearable/CGM checkboxes currently sitting in the §7 competitive matrix.
